title: Excel Automation 2026: What It Is, How to Automate Reports
summary: Excel automation handles spreadsheet refresh, cleanup, and calculations on a schedule or trigger.
body_markdown:
## Identify common Excel automation mistakes and costs


Before any script runs, the workbook underneath was already wrong in most automation failures. Audits from the 1990s found errors in 91 to 100% of the spreadsheets they examined, meaning you should assume any given sheet probably contains a mistake.


> Before any script runs, the workbook underneath was already wrong in most automation failures.


[Louise Pryor's roundup](https://www.louisepryor.com/2003/03/24/errorrates/) cites three: Coopers & Lybrand's 1997 audit found errors in 91% of the spreadsheets they examined, KPMG's 1997 audit found errors in 91%, and Lukasic's 1998 study found errors in 100%, though it covered only two spreadsheets, meaning that if your organization used spreadsheets, virtually all of them contained errors.


Automating a sheet like that doesn't fix it; it runs the error faster and on a schedule.


Treat those studies as old and narrow, since they sampled particular business spreadsheets, not every workbook. The consequence still holds: assume your file has a flaw before you wire it into anything.

### Automating a process nobody has written down


If the steps live in one person's head, the macro or flow encodes that person's habits, including the workarounds.


Before building, write the steps out: which file arrives, from whom, which columns get touched, and who approves the result. A one-page list is enough.


Skipping it means the automation breaks the first time the person who "just knows" is on leave, and nobody can say what it was supposed to do.


Write to` Sheet1!C14` from a macro and it works until someone inserts a row. Then it writes to the wrong cell and reports success. The fixes are cheap:


1. Convert data ranges to Excel tables and refer to columns by name, so inserted rows don't shift the target.
2. Use named ranges for single input cells such as a date or a threshold.
3. Add a check step that compares a row count or a total against the source and stops the run if they differ.
4. Send an alert on failure, by email or a chat message, so a broken Monday run is noticed on Monday.


Do not skip the last one. A job that fails quietly **leaves last week's numbers in place** , and people keep making decisions from them.


### Secure Excel macros and shared credentials


Treat a macro-enabled file from an unknown sender as code, not a document. Open such files only from locations you have marked as trusted, and keep Microsoft's default of blocking macros in files downloaded from the internet.


If a macro must be distributed, have it signed so recipients can see who published it.


When a flow runs on one colleague's login, or a password sits in a cell or in the macro itself, that person leaving breaks the job, and anyone who opens the file can read the secret. Credentials are the other weak point.


Use a dedicated service account with the narrowest permissions the task needs, and store the secret in the automation tool's connection settings, not in the workbook.
